title: Outbound sales plan template: A B2B example and weekly workflow
summary: Download a free outbound sales plan template with a B2B example. Set target accounts, plan outreach and review results each week.
body_markdown:
An outbound sales plan explains which accounts you will contact, why your offer could be relevant and who will handle the work. It also sets the criteria for deciding whether to keep investing in the campaign.


Those decisions are easy to leave unfinished. Researchers keep adding contacts and emails go out, but the team may still disagree about what makes a meeting useful or an opportunity worth pursuing.


Use this outbound sales plan template to settle those questions before launch. The workbook includes a blank worksheet, a completed B2B example and formulas for reviewing results.


[outbound-sales-plan-template](https://blog.floworks.ai/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/outbound-sales-plan-template.xlsx)[Download](https://blog.floworks.ai/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/outbound-sales-plan-template.xlsx)


## What’s in the outbound sales plan template?


The workbook has two tabs: Plan template and B2B example. Copy the blank tab for each campaign and fill in the amber cells. The grey cells calculate rates from your results.


Each plan has six sections:


Section What to record


Campaign brief Offer, objective, target accounts, exclusions, budget and owners


Account research Sources, observed facts, working hypothesis and next action


Outreach schedule Contact timing, follow-ups and stop conditions


Reply handling Who responds and what happens next


Cohort results Contacts reached, positive replies, meetings held and opportunities


Weekly decision log What you learned, what you will change and when to review it


The completed example follows a fictional consulting firm that offers a paid CRM workflow audit. The first invitation is for a 20-minute conversation about a routing or follow-up problem. The example numbers illustrate planning assumptions and calculations; they are not customer results or performance benchmarks.


## 1. Describe the offer in one sentence


Explain which problem you can help a buyer examine and what the first conversation will cover. Be clear about what would justify a further discussion.


The fictional campaign uses this offer:


> A 20-minute discussion to assess one lead-routing or follow-up workflow and determine whether a paid CRM workflow audit would be useful.


The researcher now has a problem to investigate, and the salesperson knows the scope of the call. The paid audit would be a separate engagement after the initial conversation about fit.


Also define what qualifies as an opportunity. For this campaign, the team needs to confirm a relevant workflow problem and its owner, along with a reason to evaluate outside help within a meaningful timeframe. A friendly reply alone would not meet those criteria.


## 2. Define which accounts and people to approach


Write account criteria that two researchers could apply consistently.


In the example, the target is US B2B software companies with 50 to 200 employees. A Head of Revenue Operations or RevOps manager may be the right contact, though the researcher still needs to check who owns the workflow at each company.


Add exclusions before building the outreach queue. Remove existing customers, active opportunities, people who have opted out and companies outside the campaign’s scope.


Your[ideal customer profile](https://blog.floworks.ai/ideal-customer-profile-template/) can supply the account criteria. Use those criteria to build a[prospect list](https://blog.floworks.ai/how-to-build-a-prospect-list/) , recording the evidence behind each selection.


Keep both documents available to the team. The campaign plan contains the selection rules; the prospect list contains the companies and contacts that meet them.


## 3. Record why each account is worth contacting now


A recent RevOps job posting that mentions lead assignment or CRM cleanup would prompt research for the example campaign. The posting gives you something to investigate. You still need to establish whether there is a buying project, an approved budget or any interest in outside help.


Separate what you found from what you think it might mean:


Research field Example


Observed fact A current RevOps role includes reviewing lead assignment workflows


Working hypothesis The company may be reconsidering how leads are routed


Missing information Who owns the work, whether it is underway and whether external help is relevant


Next action Check another relevant company source or seek confirmation in conversation


Save the original source, its date and the relevant wording so a colleague can check your reasoning without repeating the search.


If the evidence is weak, leave the account in research. The email should reflect what you know about the company, with any uncertainty kept explicit.


## 4. Choose a batch size your team can support


The example starts with research on 25 accounts and one relevant contact per approved account. That is a starting assumption for this fictional campaign. Your team’s capacity should determine your own batch size.


Allow time to review the research and messages, answer replies and take meetings. Sending capacity can be much greater than the time available to investigate an account or respond to a detailed question.


Record the approved budget for data, tools and staff time. Keep those cost definitions consistent when comparing campaigns.


If you have reliable historical results, use them to estimate the activity your goal will require. Divide the desired number of held meetings by your historical held-meeting rate to estimate how many contacts you need to reach. The earlier campaign should have a comparable audience, offer and measurement window.


Without that history, use the first batch to find out what is feasible. Label your assumptions and update them as results arrive.


## 5. Write the first message and follow-up rules


Use the research to ask a question the recipient can answer. For the fictional CRM campaign, the first email could read:


> Subject: Lead assignment at \[Company\]
>
>
> Hi \[First name\],
>
>
> Your RevOps opening mentions reviewing lead assignment workflows. Is that work already underway, or part of the incoming hire’s remit?
>
>
> We help B2B software teams review routing and follow-up workflows. If this is a current priority, would a short conversation be useful?
>
>
> \[Name\]


Check that the posting is current and supports the statement before using this example. Replace the service description with what your team provides.


The worksheet schedules the first email on day one, a follow-up on day four and a final follow-up on day nine. Adjust those intervals to the context and your team’s approved outreach practices.


A follow-up might ask about ownership:


> Hi \[First name\], following up on my question about lead assignment. Does that sit with your team, or another workflow owner?


Set the stop conditions before launch. Pause scheduled follow-ups on any reply while the team reviews it. Update suppression records after an opt-out. If you have contacted the wrong person, review the contact information before approaching someone else.


## 6. Assign an owner for each type of reply


Name the person responsible for the next action, even if one colleague covers several roles.


Response Next action


Interested Answer the question and agree on a suitable next step


Later Record the requested date and stop the current sequence


Wrong person Confirm ownership and check any suggested contact


Not interested or opt-out Stop outreach and update preferences or suppression records


Complex or unclear Route to a person who can review the context


When handing over a meeting, include the source that prompted outreach and the buyer’s response. Record the question they expect to discuss so the person taking the call can pick up the conversation where it left off.


## 7. Use consistent definitions to review results


Group contacts by when they first entered the campaign, then give each group the same observation window before comparing outcomes.


For example, you could review replies and held meetings 30 days after each contact’s first message. Your sales cycle may require a longer window for opportunities and revenue. Attribute those later updates to the original group.


The completed workbook shows an illustrative group of 80 contacts first approached:


Metric Illustrative result


Contacts reached by at least one delivered email 76


Contacts giving a positive reply 4


Contacts attending a relevant meeting 2


Unique qualified opportunities attributed to the group 1


With contacts reached as the denominator, the calculations are:


- Positive reply rate = 4 ÷ 76 × 100 = 5.3%.
- Held meeting rate = 2 ÷ 76 × 100 = 2.6%.


Count each person once for each contact metric. Leave automatic replies and unsubscribe requests out of positive replies. Track attended meetings separately from bookings, and count an opportunity once when several contacts are involved in the same deal.


To judge commercial success, you also need campaign costs, opportunity quality and eventual revenue. Use the same definitions in your[outbound sales metrics](https://blog.floworks.ai/outbound-sales-metrics/) reporting so you can follow those outcomes beyond the pilot.


## Put the plan into a weekly workflow


In week one, complete the brief and research the initial batch. Check the sources and contact ownership, then review the message before sending.


Launch the approved pilot in week two. Review replies daily and record objections or corrections in the worksheet. Investigate any deterioration in delivery or data quality before adding contacts.


By week three, look for recurring problems. Several recipients pointing you to another team would be a reason to revisit the role criteria. Questions about what you provide may call for a clearer offer description. Record each change so you can interpret the next group’s results.


At the week-four review, examine progress and costs. Keep recent contacts separate from groups that have completed the observation window. Replies and meetings from later groups may continue after the four-week pilot ends.


Write a specific next action in the decision log, with an owner. For example, “Verify workflow ownership before approving the next batch” tells the researcher what to change. A note such as “Improve targeting” still needs that decision.

## Frequently asked questions


### How is an outbound sales plan different from a prospecting list?


A prospecting list contains the accounts and people you may contact. The outbound sales plan explains why you selected them and what you will offer. It also assigns the work and defines how you will evaluate the results.


### How often should you update the plan?


Check replies and operational issues daily during an active pilot. Review campaign decisions weekly, recording the owner and reason for each change. Compare outcomes after each group has had the same amount of time to respond.


### Can a small sales team use this template?


Yes. One person can cover research, outreach and reply handling. Choose a batch size that leaves time for each responsibility, and identify any capacity gaps before increasing activity.
